---
title: "Using a Mic: A Guide for Speakers"
description: "For anyone who speaks into a mic: announcements, presentations, readings, assemblies. Slow down, say every consonant, and know what the sound engineer can and can't fix."
toc: true

This guide is for people who **speak** through a microphone: announcements, assemblies, presentations,
readings, introducing a band. You don't need to know anything about the sound system. A few habits matter
much more than the gear.

## The two most important things

**1. Slow down.** You will feel like you are speaking far too slowly. You aren't. A hall full of people
echoes: every word you say bounces around the room for a moment after you've said it. If the next word
comes too fast, it lands on top of that echo and both get smeared. "Clear speech," the kind people use to be
understood, has "a slower speaking rate, more and longer pauses" (Wikipedia, "Intelligibility").
Pause at the end of each sentence. Let the room go quiet before the next one.

**2. Say every consonant.** Vowels (a, e, o) are long and loud and survive the echo. Consonants (t, k, p, s,
d) are short and quiet, and the echo covers them up: reverberation favours "vowels with steady states, while
masking stops, glides and vowel transitions" (Wikipedia, "Intelligibility"). But the consonants are what
tell "fifteen" from "fifty," and "can" from "can't." Clear speech has "increased consonant intensity compared
to adjacent vowels" (same source). Finish the ends of words. Over-pronounce a little: what sounds fussy up
close sounds normal at the back of the room.

<div class="sk-tip">Try it: read one sentence at your normal speed, then again at about two-thirds the speed,
hitting every final t and d. Record both on your phone from across the room and listen back.</div>

Numbers, names and times are the easiest things to lose. Say them slowly, and say the important ones twice:
"Room two-oh-four. That's two, oh, four."

## Holding a handheld mic

- **Close, and the same distance all the time.** A few centimetres to about a hand's width from your mouth.
  The closer the mic, the more of you and the less of the room it hears (Wikipedia, "Gain before feedback").
  The level changes fast with distance: halve the distance and you are about 6 dB louder. Keep the
  distance steady and the engineer can set you once.
- **Point it at your mouth**, not at your chin or chest. Most mics hear from the end, not the side.
- **Turn your head with the mic.** If you look at someone on your left, take the mic with you.
- **Very close sounds boomy.** Right on your lips the mic adds bass (the **proximity effect**: Wikipedia,
  "Proximity effect"). A little is warm; a lot is muddy.
- **Pops.** "P" and "b" push a puff of air into the mic and it thumps. Hold the mic slightly below or to the
  side of your mouth, so you speak across it, not straight into it.
- **Hold the handle**, not the ball at the top. Covering the grille muffles the sound and can cause feedback.
- **Don't tap it or blow into it** to check it's on. Just say "Good morning" at your normal level.

## On a stand or a lectern

Adjust the stand before you start, not halfway through. Bring the mic to your mouth, not your mouth to the mic.
At a lectern, keep the same distance when you look down at your notes: lean with the mic, or lift your notes.
If you move away from the lectern, you have left the mic.

## Clip-on (lavalier) and headset mics

- A clip-on mic goes in the middle of your chest, a hand's width below your chin, on the outside of your
  clothes. Scarves, jackets and lanyards rubbing on it are very loud.
- Turning your head away from it makes you quieter. Talk forward.
- Before you go on: ask where the mute switch is. Assume the mic is always on. People in the hall hear
  backstage conversations.

## Walking around

Don't walk in front of the loudspeakers with a live mic. A mic pointed at a speaker hears itself,
the sound goes round the loop, and it squeals: **feedback** (Wikipedia, "Audio feedback"). If it starts
squealing, step back behind the speakers or turn the mic away. Don't cover it with your hand.

## What the sound engineer can and can't do

The engineer has a lot of tools, but they all work on the sound that reaches the mic. They can't put back
what the mic never heard.

| The engineer **can** | The engineer **can't** |
|---|---|
| Set your level so you are clear, if you stay at a steady distance | Make you loud when the mic is far away. Turning up a distant mic turns up the room too, and it squeals before you are loud enough (Wikipedia, "Gain before feedback") |
| Take some boominess out of your voice with EQ, and cut low rumble | Make a mumbled word clear, or separate two words you ran together |
| Smooth out some loud/soft swings with a compressor | Keep up with a sudden shout after a whisper. Shouting into the mic just distorts. Step back instead |
| Reduce pops a little with a low cut | Remove a pop completely. Speak across the mic |
| Turn you up for the room, and mute you between speakers | Know you're about to speak. Tell them your cue, and don't start until you hear yourself |
| Fix feedback by turning you down | Turn you back up while you're standing in front of the speakers |
| Help you before the event, at a sound check | Fix in the moment what a two-minute sound check would have caught |

The engineer can only turn up what's there. A clear, steady voice can be made bigger. A muddled one only
becomes louder and muddled.

## Before you speak: a checklist

1. **Sound check.** Say a sentence or two at the level you'll really use (not quieter, and not "check one two").
2. Ask the engineer: is the mic on now? Who switches it on?
3. Find your distance and keep it.
4. Mark slow-down and pause points in your notes.
5. Practise the names and numbers out loud.
6. Water nearby. A dry mouth loses consonants first.
